Part III - Data management¶

Part III - Data management. Section 1: the data model.

Theory¶

A reconstruction task has four kinds of information, and keeping them apart is the organising principle of the whole package.

  1. Specification (Experiment). What is the sample made of and how is it imaged? It consists of

    • the imaging setup \(\mathcal{I}\) - mode (TEM or STEM-HAADF), image shape \((H, W)\), pixel size \(\Delta x\), acceleration voltage \(U\), aberration coefficients, envelope, detector;

    • the layer stack - an ordered list of slices \(\ell = 1 \dots L\) with element, height \(z_\ell\), and membership in a group;

    • the groups - rigid units that move together (global shift, rotation, scale, a smooth strain field);

    • the initial atomic structure, one list of positions per layer (Eq. 3.1: \(\mathbf{r}_{\ell,i} \in \mathbb{R}^2\), in pixels).

  2. Trainable state (ModelState). The numbers the optimiser changes: per-atom position shifts \(\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell,i}\), intensity (a continuous atomic number) \(Z_{\ell,i}\), occupancy logit \(o_{\ell,i}\), per-group transformation and strain control points, and the microscope parameters. The effective position of an atom is

    \[\mathbf{r}^{\rm eff}_{\ell,i} = \mathbf{r}_{\ell,i} + \delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell,i} \qquad (3.2)\]

    so the specification is never overwritten by training.

  3. Training settings (TrainSettings). Which parts of the state may change, with which learning rate, how the loss terms are weighted, how strongly regularisers act, and which image regions count. This is policy, not physics.

  4. Observations (the target image and masks). Bulk arrays; they live in .npy/.npz files next to the JSON, marked external below.

Implementation¶

All classes are dataclasses without behaviour beyond validation and lookup. They import nothing but numpy, so that the user interface process can use them without loading torch. temsim.data.codec converts them to and from JSON; temsim.data.store puts them on disk; temsim.data.legacy reads the formats of earlier versions.

Units: lengths in the structure are pixels (origin at the image corner), heights z_nm and the pixel size in nanometres, aberration coefficients in the units of temsim.physics.optics (documented there), angles in mrad or rad as named.

Generic conversion between dataclasses and JSON-compatible values.

Every persistent object in temsim.data.schema is a plain dataclass. Rather than writing a to_dict/from_dict pair per class, one pair of functions walks the type annotations:

  • encode turns a dataclass tree into dicts, lists, numbers and strings,

  • decode rebuilds the tree from such values, guided by the target class.

Rules¶

  • numpy arrays become nested lists and come back as float64 arrays,

  • tuples become lists and come back as tuples where the annotation says so,

  • fields marked metadata={"external": True} hold bulk arrays (masks, target images) that live in .npz files; they are skipped here,

  • unknown keys are ignored by default so that a file written by a newer version still loads; pass strict=True to turn them into errors.

Part III, Section 2: the data-folder convention.

Theory¶

A measurement is a folder. Convention (every item optional unless stated):

<folder>/
    target.tif | target.npy       the measured image (required)
    mask_<group>.tif | <group>_mask.tif | mask.tif
                                  region in which atoms of <group> are expected
    init.json | init_random.json  setup (pixel size, voltage, mode, lattices ...)
    <config_dir>/                 run directories written by the programs

The image is dimensionless; Part II normalises it (Eq. 5.1), so the file’s grey values are irrelevant except for one defect: detectors write exact zeros for pixels that were never read. Those would pull the minimum of the image to zero and distort the normalisation, therefore target_zero_handling == "median" (the default, as in the ImageJ plug-in) replaces exact zeros by the image median.

init.json is written by the ImageJ plug-in (version 2) and, in reduced form, by the headless seeding command (init_random.json). Length units in it follow the plug-in’s conventions (shift in pixels, rotation in degrees); this module converts to the internal convention of temsim.data.schema (radians). Turning lattice recipes into atoms is physics and lives in temsim.physics.structure.

Part III, Section 3: persistence and versioning.

Theory¶

A run directory is the unit of reproducibility. It holds exactly the objects of the data model (temsim.data.schema):

experiment.json   Experiment    the specification, incl. initial atoms
train.json        TrainSettings policy (without bulk arrays)
state.json        ModelState    trained numbers (optional)
masks.npz         masks by group name          (optional)
targets.npz       group targets by group name  (optional)
target.npy        the measured image           (optional)

Together they determine a run up to the random seed (Section 4: seeds are part of train.json once a seeding run has used them).

Versioning follows one rule. Every JSON file carries schema_version; files of the current version are decoded by the generic codec, everything else is routed to temsim.data.legacy. Legacy detection is structural, not by file name, because the old programs wrote files without any version marker:

  • experiment: "imaging" key present -> current, "init_positions" -> legacy;

  • train settings: nested "loss" object -> current, otherwise legacy;

  • model state: "position_shifts" at the top level -> current, "potential_parameters" -> legacy.

For reading, the file names of the old programs are also understood (config.json, train_method.json, area_masks.npz/.npy, group_targets.npz, target_gr.npy); on writing only the new names are used. Writing is atomic (temporary file, then rename) so that an interrupted save never leaves half a file behind.

Part III, Section 3: reading the formats of earlier versions.

Theory¶

A file format is a contract that outlives the code that wrote it. Four formats exist in the wild, and all of them must stay readable:

File

Generations

config.json

(a) fixed four layers Gr/S1/W/S2 with z_positions_nm and control_points_*; (b) layers/groups; each either written with asdict or wrapped as {"__type__": "dataclass", ...}.

train_method.json

(a) flat flags graphen_shift …; (b) groups/layers dictionaries; plain or wrapped.

parameter dumps

scale_Gr, shift_WS2, graphene_potential_factor

(best.json …)

or the group dictionaries; polar or cartesian aberrations.

init.json

written by the ImageJ plug-in (input, version 1 and 2).

Strategy (Eq. 3.3): a migration is a pure function from the raw JSON value to the current schema, new = M_k(M_{k-1}(...(old))). Nothing in the rest of the code knows an old name. Every function here has a test that loads real files.

Aberration coefficients are passed through unchanged: converting between the polar and the cartesian form is optics, not data management (see temsim.physics.optics). Likewise, resampling a strain control grid to a different resolution happens where the grid is applied.
